To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Low family income in childhood is associated with educational and economic disadvantage in adulthood, but is not directly associated with increased risks of crime and mental health problems, nor with teen pregnancy".

low family income during the first decade of life is associated with a wide range of negative developmental outcomes in adulthood, but that these negative associations are largely explained by the social, family and contextual factors that are correlated, both directly and indirectly, with low family income.

(a) low family income during the first 18 years of life is associated with a wide range of negative life outcomes in adulthood, (b) the associations between childhood income and these outcomes are mediated by social, family and child characteristics that are correlated with income and contribute to negative developmental outcomes in adulthood, and (c) the associations between income and educational achievement and economic status persist after covariate adjustment but are not significant for the other outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between economic circumstances in the family of origin and the developmental outcomes of the children.
how childhood experiences of family economic circumstances influence later developmental outcomes.
the long-term impact of economic circumstances during childhood on later life outcomes, and the mechanisms through which this impact occurs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the association of low childhood family income with a range of developmental outcomes is not due to the direct impact of low family income but is due to the indirect impact of low family economic status on other social, family and personal characteristics that are correlated with family income and are associated with the developmental outcomes.

the relationship between family income and the outcomes of interest in the present study is mediated, at least in part, by a range of other factors that are associated with low family income, and which contribute to the observed associations between childhood family income and the later outcomes.

the association between childhood family economic conditions and later outcomes is mediated by a complex web of individual, family and environmental factors that are correlated and causally related to low family income and that contribute to later outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while there are clear and important associations between childhood family income and a range of developmental outcomes spanning educational attainment; crime; mental well-being; and teenage pregnancy, after controlling for other important factors these associations are no longer significant.
the association between childhood family income and subsequent developmental outcomes is mediated by a range of individual, family and contextual factors.

, in this cohort, childhood family income was not a direct determinant of adult mental health problems, offending or teenage pregnancy, but was a significant determinant of educational achievement and economic outcomes in adulthood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between childhood economic circumstances and later developmental outcomes is complex and mediated by individual, familial and social contextual factors.

, after taking account of a number of important social, family and personal characteristics that may be correlated with childhood family income, low family income is associated with a number of negative life outcomes in adulthood.

, after due account is taken of the social and family contexts in which individuals are reared and the individual attributes they bring to the situation, low family income is associated with educational and economic disadvantage, but does not directly contribute to increased risks of offending, mental health problems and teenage pregnancy.
